also: what are we having for dinner?

terms.grammar: quid with the partitive genitive; for the other meals jentāculī, prandiī
evidence: Ter. Haut. 211–212: ut videam nōbīs quid cēnae siet
terms.comment: Terence’s old man goes indoors “to see what we have for dinner”: quid with the genitive asks what there is of a thing, as quid novī? asks for news. The same question serves the other meals: Quid jentāculī est?, Quid prandiī est?.

terms.gloss: what are we having for dinner?
terms.comment: Trimalchio asks a guest what they had at a dinner: habēre in cēnā is Petronius’s own idiom, not an English calque.

phrases.latin: Ego ībō hinc intrō, ut videam nōbīs quid cēnae siet.
phrases.english: I’ll go in and see what we have for dinner.
what did you have at dinner?

phrases.latin: Quid cēnae est, tata? — Pullus et pīsa.
phrases.english: What’s for dinner, Dad? — Chicken and peas.

phrases.latin: Quid jentāculī est? — Puls cum melle.
phrases.english: What’s for breakfast? — Porridge with honey.

sources: Lewis & Short: cena
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 304.
